signals.summary: Sustained demand for at-home training gear - racks, Smith machines, rowers, ellipticals, saunas - turns the home gym into an object-and-interior story. Pure equipment and space, no bodies required.
signals.why_now: Hurriyet reports a home-workout trend boosting fitness equipment sales; Breaking Muscle runs a steady evergreen stream of gear roundups (best power rack, Smith machine, compact rowing machine, elliptical, outdoor sauna).

signals.summary: A visible pivot away from grind-cardio toward Pilates, 'doing less', exercise snacks and ultra-low-intensity work. Reads visually as reformer studios, mats and calm morning-light rooms.
signals.why_now: Health.com covers STRONG Pilates as the latest Pilates-inspired format; ELLE frames a workout trend that 'makes a case for doing less'; Us Weekly explains 'exercise snacks' for gym-avoiders; NY Post pushes 'Zone 0' exercise; Men's Journal notes a shift away from high-calorie-burn cardio.

signals.summary: Hyrox, the mass-participation functional fitness race, keeps spreading globally and is repeatedly framed as 'the new CrossFit'. Best shown through the kit and arena - sleds, sandbags, wall balls, rowing ergs on a competition floor - rather than faces.
signals.why_now: Independent outlets keep covering the same wave: DW on how Germany's Hyrox became a global craze, USA Today asking if it is the new CrossFit, The Times on Chinese pensioners joining, plus ABC News and Yahoo explainers.

signals.summary: A broad 'move like you're younger' wave: mobility drills, stretching and functional-strength work for aging well. Producible through bands, mats and foam rollers in a studio, though it leans on body demonstration.
signals.why_now: Outside runs 8 mobility moves to move younger, Tom's Guide and Katie Couric cover functional strength for seniors, Runner's World targets runners over 50, the NYT lists exercises PTs wish everyone did to age well, plus WBAL, Woman & Home and Health.com stretch pieces.

signals.summary: Sleep optimization as a wellness ritual expressed through the bedroom itself - cool dim rooms, premium mattress covers, legs-up-the-wall and bedtime flows. All environment and object, no faces.
signals.why_now: University of Utah Health explains why a cooler bedroom helps sleep; Fortune profiles the high-end mattress-cover company; Yoga With Adriene posts legs-up-the-wall and a 10-minute bedtime flow; a sleep doctor flags summer habits wrecking rest.

signals.summary: Group and community-driven workouts keep being framed as the mood shift in how people train. Fits the category but is inherently crowd- and body-led, so it produces poorly for a face-free studio.
signals.why_now: NY Post covers a group fitness trend getting New Yorkers in their best shape; Medscape asks if Gen Z group workouts are better; Men's Journal ties a group fitness trend to a broader shift in how we think about health; CBS covers 'kidulting' fun-fitness gyms.
